entries.meaning: Vibhishana has stated policy approved by wise people, the Puranas, and the Vedas. Hearing it, Ravana springs up enraged: death is now near the villain who has always lived through Ravana's protection yet favors the enemy. He boasts that no one in the world remains unconquered by his arms and tells Vibhishana, who lives in his city but loves the ascetics, to go join them and preach policy to them. Ravana kicks him, while his younger brother repeatedly holds his feet. Shiva tells Uma that this is the greatness of a saint: he does good even to one who does evil. Vibhishana says Ravana is like a father and may rightly strike him, but Ravana's welfare lies in worshiping Rama. Taking his ministers, he rises into the sky and publicly declares that Rama's resolve is true and Ravana's assembly is in Time's power; he is going to Raghubira for refuge, and no one should blame him.

The moment Vibhishana departs, the others become bereft of longevity. Shiva tells Bhavani that contempt for a saint immediately destroys every good. When Ravana rejects Vibhishana, the unfortunate king at once loses his splendor. Vibhishana joyfully goes toward Raghunatha, forming many hopes in his mind: he will see those red, tender, joy-giving lotus feet whose touch carried the sage's wife Ahalya across and sanctified the Dandaka forest; the feet Sita held to her heart when Rama ran after the deceptive deer; the lotus feet in the lake of Shiva's heart. He marvels that he will see with his own eyes the very feet upon whose sandals Bharata fixed his mind.

Reflecting lovingly in this way, Vibhishana quickly reaches the near shore of the sea. The monkeys see him coming and take him for a special enemy agent. They detain him and report everything to Sugriva, who tells Rama that Ravana's brother has come to meet him. Asked for his view, Sugriva warns that a shape-shifting demon's design cannot be known: the villain has come to obtain their secrets and should be bound. Rama calls the policy well considered, but states his own vow to remove the fear of anyone who seeks refuge. Hanuman rejoices on hearing that the Lord cherishes those who surrender. People who abandon a refugee because they infer danger to themselves are base and steeped in sin; merely seeing them causes harm.

Even if the guilt of killing ten million Brahmins clings to someone, Rama says, he will not abandon that person when they come for refuge. The moment a being turns toward him, the sins of millions of births perish. A sinner's natural disposition has no liking for Rama's worship, so a truly wicked-hearted person could not sincerely approach him. Only a person of pure mind finds him; deceit, fraud, and fault-finding do not please him. Even if the ten-headed king sent Vibhishana for intelligence, Sugriva need fear no loss: Lakshmana can destroy in an instant every demon in the world. If Vibhishana has come frightened and seeking refuge, Rama will protect him like his own life. Smiling, the abode of compassion tells them to bring him in either case, and Angada goes with Hanuman while all acclaim the merciful Lord.

The monkeys respectfully lead Vibhishana toward compassionate Raghupati. From afar he sees the two brothers, givers of delight to the eyes; then he beholds Rama, abode of beauty, and stops transfixed for a moment. Rama's long arms, red-lotus eyes, dark body, and refuge-giving form dispel fear; his lion shoulders and broad chest shine, and his face captivates even countless minds of Love. With tearful eyes and a profoundly thrilled body, Vibhishana steadies himself and speaks gently: he is the ten-headed Ravana's brother, born in the demon lineage, with a tamasic body naturally fond of sin as an owl loves darkness. Hearing the Lord's fair fame has brought him to the destroyer of worldly fear. He begs Raghubira, remover of distress and giver of refuge's joy, to save him.

Seeing Vibhishana prostrate as he speaks, the delighted Lord immediately rises. Pleased by the humble words, Rama takes him in his vast arms and embraces him, then seats him nearby with Lakshmana. The remover of his devotees' fear asks the new lord of Lanka whether he and his family are well while dwelling in so harsh a place, and how he maintains dharma while living day and night among the wicked. Rama knows all his ways: Vibhishana is highly skilled in policy and does not love injustice. Better to live in hell, Rama says, than for fate to give one the company of villains. Vibhishana replies that he is well now that he has seen Raghuraya's feet and the Lord has knowingly shown mercy to his servant. A being has neither welfare nor even dreamlike rest in the mind until, abandoning desire—the abode of grief—it worships Rama.

Greed, delusion, envy, arrogance, and pride inhabit the heart only until Raghunatha, holding bow, arrows, and a quiver at his waist, dwells there. Attachment is a young and deeply dark night in which the owls of attraction and aversion flourish, but only until the sun of the Lord's majesty rises in a being's mind. Vibhishana is now well and his heavy fears have vanished after seeing Rama's lotus feet. The threefold pains of worldly existence cannot touch one to whom the merciful Lord is favorable. Vibhishana calls himself a demon of extremely low disposition who has performed no good conduct, yet the Lord whose form eludes the sages' meditation has joyfully embraced him. His fortune is measureless: by Rama's grace his eyes have seen the pair of lotus feet served by Brahma and Shiva.

Rama tells his friend his own nature, known to Kakabhushundi, Shiva, and Girija. If even an enemy of all moving and unmoving creation comes fearfully and seeks refuge in him, abandoning arrogance, delusion, pretense, and every deceit, Rama immediately makes that person like a saint. One should gather every thread of possessive attachment—to mother, father, kin, child, spouse, body, wealth, home, friends, and family—and use the strong cord to bind the mind to his feet. Such an even-sighted person wants nothing and has no joy, grief, or fear in the mind. Such saints dwell in Rama's heart as wealth dwells in a miser's. Saints like Vibhishana are dear to him; he assumes a body for no other obligation. Those who worship his manifest form, devote themselves to others' welfare, remain firm in policy and discipline, and love the feet of Brahmins are as dear to him as life.

Rama tells the new lord of Lanka that all these virtues are his and therefore he is exceedingly dear. The monkey hosts acclaim the mass of compassion. Vibhishana cannot be sated by the nectar of Rama's words; repeatedly clasping the lotus feet, his boundless love will not fit within his heart. He addresses the Lord of moving and unmoving creation, protector of the surrendered and knower within hearts: some desire had remained there before, but it has now flowed away in the river of love for the Lord's feet. He asks for Rama's own purifying devotion, always dear to Shiva's mind, and Rama grants it. The battle-valiant Lord asks at once for ocean water and explains that, although his friend has no desire, his own sight is unfailing; with that water he anoints Vibhishana, and flowers rain boundlessly from the sky. Rama has saved Vibhishana from the fire of Ravana's anger, fanned fiercely by his breath, and given him an undivided kingdom. The very wealth Shiva gave Ravana for the offering of ten heads, Raghunatha gives Vibhishana almost bashfully.

Those who abandon such a Lord and worship another are humans only as tailless, hornless animals. Rama accepts Vibhishana as his own servant, and the Lord's nature delights the monkey race. Then the omniscient indweller of every heart—present in every form yet detached from all—speaks as a guardian of proper policy, having taken human form for a purpose and to destroy the demon race. He asks Sugriva and the valiant lord of Lanka how the deep ocean, crowded with crocodiles, serpents, and fish, and unfathomable and difficult in every way, should be crossed. Vibhishana replies that Rama's arrows can dry up ten million oceans; nevertheless, policy prescribes that he first make a respectful request to the Ocean. The sea is an ancestral preceptor of Rama's line and will consider and state a means by which the whole host of bears and monkeys can cross without effort.
